newsitem.title: ISRAEL: No-taxes pledge may fall in Israel budget battle.
newsitem.headline: No-taxes pledge may fall in Israel budget battle.

text.p: Faced with widespread opposition in parliament and undisciplined coalition partners, Israel's Treasury will backtrack on a no-new-taxes pledge to get approval of 1997 budget cuts, analysts said on Tuesday.

"In the end, parliament will accept (the budget cuts), especially if they are accompanied by new taxes," former treasury budget director Yoram Gabbay, now chairmain of Peilim fund managers, told Reuters.
The Treasury was already facing widespread opposition from lawmakers over the 4.9 billion shekels in budget cuts contained in the original 1997 budget unveiled last October.
The second round of spending cuts approved by the cabinet on Monday will face even tougher opposition.

The plan for new cuts totalling 1.2 billion shekels also calls for 600 million shekels in additional income from non-tax sources, such as the sale of state-owned homes in the occupied West Bank and higher penalties for motor vehicle violations.
Financial consultant and former budget director David Boas warned that the atmosphere in parliament was bad for legislative deal making.
"Everyone suspects everyone else. They don't believe anyone. No one gives any weight to any promises," he said.
He said it was possible the government would fail to win parliament's approval by December 31.
In that case, by law, the 1996 budget remains in force for three months, after which the government falls automatically if a new budget has not been passed.
Budget critics in parliament and among Netanyahu's own ministers say the spending cuts will fall hardest on lower-income groups.

In past years, the government would have had an easier time imposing party discipline, but internal party primaries and direct election of the prime minister -- two recent political reforms -- have undermined the old system.

"There is a general situation in (parliament), which is very different than previous parliaments, in that the small parties have a lot of power," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist with Solid Financial Markets.
That will force Finance Minister Dan Meridor to compromise by replacing some spending cuts with new or higher taxes.
"He will get his cuts in the end, but I assume it will include one to 1.5 billion shekels in new taxes," said Gabbay. "It's not realistic to expect cuts in defence, child allowances or health."
Cuts in child allowances and higher fees for doctor visits are two of the most controversial parts of the original 4.9 billion shekels in cuts.
Analysts say Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has supported Meridor on the budget but is determined to increase defence spending.

They noted that the second-round spending-cut package approved by the cabinet on Monday does not specify the cuts, only that each ministry must slash a certain percentage. The ministers are to have their proposals ready by week's end.
"At this stage, it's a decision in principle not in details," said Gabbay. "The test will be in the particulars."
He said once legislators knew which line items were destined for the axe, opposition would coalesce.
Boas said they would use the post-December 31 period as the time for what he called "maximum blackmail position".
($1 = 3.28 shekels)
